title: Majestic Domain Expansion
reviewNotes: All 61 saved states and narration reviewed. The study starts after ...Ka4 at 45s in the seven-piece diagram White Kb2/Qe3/Ne4/b7/e2 versus Black Ka4/Qb6. Earlier eight-piece bishop defense and queen offers remain source context. Five checked branches cover Qxb6 stalemate, Kc2/...Qxb7/Nc5 fork, Kc2/...Qxe3/Nc3+/Ka3/b8=B and the decoy-to-fork win, b8=Q/...Qd2+/Kxd2 stalemate, and the bishop mate after ...Qh3. No proof claim is made for the earlier eight-piece choices.
transcript: White brilliantly sacrifices the queen, because if the queen is captured, now he could get a new queen with check and then pick up the black bishop, winning the game. But black is not that naive, and instead of capturing the white queen, he plays bishop to E3, maintaining the pressure on the queen while also keeping an eye on the pawn, meaning that promoting now would leave the players to an equal position. But of course, bishop to E3 doesn't seem to make sense, because white can just re-sacrifice the queen, since sacrificed queen would lead down a similar win for white. But you see, black had foreseen the queen sacrifice, and he was just trying to get rid of his pieces, so that he could play the brilliant king to A4, leaving the queens in a standoff. Both of them are free for the taking, but neither of them can be captured, because if white takes this queen, this would actually be a stalemate, a situation where there are no legal moves, but the black king is not checkmated. So, this would be a draw. But don't forget that chess is not checkers, and white is under no obligation to capture that black queen, and he can instead sacrifice his queen for the third time in a row with the majestic king to C2, because surprisingly, the pawn is untouchable. This would run into a knight fork, winning the end game for white. And if black takes the queen, we should still now be able to promote, right? Well, not exactly. This time the promotion [music] doesn't come with a check, so black would be able to pick up the white knight, and incredibly, even if white tries to save the knight with a check first, after the king moves, we still cannot get a queen, because out of nowhere, black will play queen to D2, sacrificing the last of his pieces, because of course, once the queen is taken, this is going to be yet another stalemate and so it seems that black is finally out of the woods but a shiver goes down the spine of the player with the black pieces. As white plays the sublime and incredibly rare promotion to a bishop. And it all [music] comes tumbling down because bishop to D6 is a surprising >> [music] >> checkmate threat and amazingly enough the black queen has no safe checks to deliver thanks to the [music] white knight. But black is not just going to resign. He has a queen for a knight and a bishop. Surely this is still winning. He just needs to defend the D6 square but unfortunately any move that defends this square will not stop bishop to D6. This would be a checkmate. The black queen has to take but yet again the king and the queen find themselves in an awkward position that allows knight to B5 with a fork. The queen will fall and white will win this game. [music]
